podcast.body: This most famous Joy Division track was one of their last, recorded in March 1980 by producer Martin Hannett at Strawberry studio outside Manchester. It was released on June 27, 1980, approximately five weeks after lead singer Ian Curtis took his own life. The song originated from an August 1979 jam session, with Curtis's lyrics reflecting the intense turmoil of his life, including worsening epilepsy exacerbated by various lifestyle factors, a failing marriage to Deborah, and an affair with Anaconda Rae. Despite its happy-sounding, major key arrangement that initially puzzled the band, its profound lyrical depth and Hannett's meticulous production make it a poignant reflection of Curtis's final weeks, leading it to be called Joy Division's "Suicide Note Song." "It wouldn't be released until June 27, 1980, about five weeks after singer Ian Curtis took his own life."

podcast.body: This song is hailed as one of the most important modern songs ever written. Due to the band's strong belief in its future significance for their career, they recorded it extensively, "a million times in a million places." The definitive version was recorded at Strawberry Studios, although earlier versions were also made at BBC studios. Prior to its release, Joy Division had a relative critical presence but struggled to gain widespread recognition or significant record sales. The band invested enormous effort from the outset, convinced it would make them stars, especially as they were already gaining strong momentum and preparing for their first US tour. They tested the song live during tours in late 1979 and early 1980, with extant recordings revealing subtle nuances and differences in the famous background melody, which they continuously refined. Its lyrics are rooted in Ian Curtis's tragic emotional turmoil, caught between his wife and a lover whom he did not desire but who made his life difficult. The title of the song is famously inscribed on Ian Curtis's gravestone. It holds the unique distinction of being the only song where Ian Curtis played guitar, albeit poorly, just a few chords, as he was not a musician. It is also the only music video the group ever made. The song was released approximately five or six times, achieving notable success upon its 1980 release, but truly became an anthem throughout the 1980s. It is recognized as one of the most covered and enduring singles in music history, comparable to major works by Pink Floyd, Michael Jackson, or The Beatles. Following its publication, Ian Curtis lived for three more months, during which the single began to achieve relative success, but his subsequent death led to the cancellation of the band's impending US tour. "la grabaron un millón de veces en un millón de sitios."
